vignette: The sandstorm hits before the sound. One moment he is riding in the back of an MRAP, the radio crackling with static from a comrade two hundred yards ahead. The next, the world detonates. Heat washes over his face. Shrapnel tears through the cabin air. He wakes up three days later in a field hospital, the taste of copper and dust heavy in his throat. He is twenty years old then. Now, at twenty-four, Mateo sits in a glass-walled conference room downtown, the hum of HVAC systems masking the distant wail of sirens. He works as a financial analyst for a mid-sized firm in Chicago. His job requires him to untangle quarterly forecasts, model risk exposure, and present projections to clients who expect calm certainty. Mateo delivers the numbers with a steady voice, but beneath his desk, his left foot taps a frantic, uneven rhythm. He has learned to sit facing the door. He has learned to notice the fire extinguishers and the nearest staircase in every room he enters. The transition from base to apartment is supposed to be clean. Instead, the silence of his studio becomes a pressure. At night, the refrigerator’s compressor kicks on and his jaw locks. He lies awake, counting his breaths until the ceiling fan sounds like rotor wash. During the day, spreadsheets blur when a car backfires outside the office window. His chest tightens, his vision narrows, and for three seconds he is back in the dust, waiting for the next strike. He blinks, checks the time, and quietly exits the elevator to the stairwell. He does not tell his supervisor. He tells himself he is fine. He tells himself he is just tired. His colleagues praise his analytical precision. They do not see how he uses risk models as a shield. If he can predict the market, he reasons, he can control what comes next. He stays late at the office, running sensitivity analyses on unrelated portfolios, chasing the illusion of order. When clients ask about his weekend, he gives short answers and checks his watch. He has not returned a call from his mother in Guadalajara in two months. He lets his dating app notifications stack unread, telling himself he is better off alone until he figures out how to sit through a dinner without scanning the exit. When he does speak to his mother, his voice stays flat, as though emotion might crack the line. He misses the familiar cadence of Spanish, the weight of his father’s expectations, the way his tía used to press calms into his hands during childhood storms. Instead, he has a half-empty gym bag, a subscription to a sleep app, and a growing list of client meetings he reschedules. In his fifth session, he describes waking at 3 a.m. on a Tuesday, drenched in sweat, convinced his bedroom door has just been breached. He checks the locks twice. He sits on the floor until his heartbeat slows enough for him to remember where he is. He speaks about the numbers as if they are the only things that do not lie. He describes the way his hands tremble when a colleague drops a stack of folders. He does not cry. He does not ask for help. He simply waits for the therapist to ask the next question.
